claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys have superior structural and chemical stability at high temperatures compared with lower-entropy nanoalloys.
Large configurational entropy flattens the free-energy landscape of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Flattening of the free-energy landscape increases barriers to atomic diffusion.
Increased atomic-diffusion barriers suppress phase segregation.
Increased atomic-diffusion barriers suppress grain growth.
Grain-boundary composition and complex multi-element interactions govern atomic-diffusion barriers.
Elevated diffusion activation energy suppresses grain-boundary migration.
Elevated diffusion activation energy suppresses elemental segregation and associated structural degradation.
After equivalent high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single-phase microstructure better than the lower-entropy control.
After equivalent high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than the lower-entropy control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit a higher diffusion activation energy than the lower-entropy control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will show less phase separation after high-temperature exposure than the lower-entropy control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will show less grain growth after high-temperature exposure than the lower-entropy control.
The prediction is limited to nanoalloys that are initially homogeneous and single phase.
Melting or substantial surface reconstruction can override the proposed entropy-stabilization effect.
